catalog_quote: § 25. The accentuation in native ME. words was essentially the same as in OE., that is, in all uncompounded words the chief accent fell upon the stem-syllable and always remained there even when suffixes and inflexional endings followed it. In compound words the chief accent fell upon the stem-syllable of the first component part if the second part was a noun or an adjective; and on the stem-syllable of the second part if this was a verb or derived from a verb. ... § 186. The O.Fr. and AN. accented vowels in early borrowed words, which became post-tonic in ME. through shifting of the accent, remained for a time unchanged, and then later became weakened down through loss of the new secondary accent ... § 215. The O.Fr. and AN. pretonic vowels and diphthongs which became tonic (accented) through the shifting of the accent generally remained in ME.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Middle English carries an empty rule; this work supplies the placement (stem-initial / leftmost-foot main stress, continuing Old English) and the loanword exceptions, consistent with the 'morphological' kind our list of works to obtain assigns to the record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Middle English kept the Old English (Germanic) stress system: main stress on the stem-initial syllable regardless of syllable weight (certain prefixes unstressed), with Germanic Feet built left to right and main stress on the leftmost foot; the Old-to-Middle English changes (Final Destressing, Final Consonant Extrametricality, Trisyllabic Shortening) did not move main stress, they only shortened words metrically. Directionality and main-stress position did not change before 1530.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress built from left to right by Germanic Feet (ms. p.2 (1)); Old English (and by continuity ME) 'lacked secondary stress in final syllables' (ms. p.8, (15)); Final Destressing / Final Consonant Extrametricality account for the lack of final secondary stress in the transition to ME (ms. p.9, (16)-(17)).
new_statements.exceptions: Romance loans could show French stress (final, or penult if final is schwa) in Chaucer's verse, but 'could in general also be stressed according to the native English pattern, as required by the meter', giving doublets citee ~ citee, comfort ~ comfort, divers ~ diverse, geaunt ~ geant, Plato ~ Plato, present ~ present (ms. p.5 (7)); PDE reflexes of these words have initial stress 'with very few exceptions' (degree, divine, reward: ms. p.5); the authors reject Halle & Keyser's (1971) claim that a Romance stress rule entered English in Chaucer's time (ms. pp.6-7).
new_statements.identity_note: Dresher & Lahiri 2005 is explicitly about early Middle English (title) with loan data from Chaucer's late-14th-century London English; Dresher 2013 and Dresher & Lahiri 2022 cover the whole ME period to c.1530/1570; Wardale is a general ME handbook with no dialect restriction. No source describes a specific ME dialect's stress as differing.

new_statements.rule_in_words: From Germanic through Middle English, feet were built from the left and main stress fell on the leftmost foot (i.e. word-initial main stress); foot direction only began changing to the right c.1570 and main stress moved rightward c.1660 onward. The Anglo-Norman/Old French loanword influx after the Conquest made little impact on Middle English prosody.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stresses follow from the left-to-right Germanic Foot (an extended, resolved trochee) that the authors argue held through the ME period (abstract; sec. 3).
new_statements.exceptions: Latin loanwords with stress-affecting suffixes (-able, -ation, -ion, -ity..) are counted for 1400 vs 1570 (ms. p.11, (15)); they only tip the system after 1570, i.e. after the ME period.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as works 1-2 (initial/stem main stress unchanged through ME); adds the explicit unstressed-prefix clause, secondary-stress remarks and the short list of final-stressed loan exceptions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the initial (stem) syllable, certain prefixes unstressed, Germanic Feet built left to right with main stress on the leftmost foot; this Old English system persisted unchanged through Middle English (to c.1530) despite the Romance loan influx, the loans being assimilated to initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Native trisyllables like martyrdom, maidenhod, tonneful, stedefast(e) 'may have had secondary stresses on the third syllable, especially when it was not word final, as in Old English; hence, stedefast ~ stedefaste' (p.60 n.8); in OE a final heavy syllable with no dependent is defooted and 'receives no secondary stress' (p.58, (6c) and (7e)).
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressed prefixes (lexically marked, p.58 n.4; Romance verbs with prefix-like initial syllables fit this pattern, p.60 citing Minkova 2006:114); disyllabic Romance loans borrowed before 1500 with final stress in PDE: diverse (1297), reward (1340), divine (1374), degree (1380) (p.60, (12c)); ME siment had initial stress until the 19th c. (p.61, (14)).

new_statements.quote: p.3: "English, like all Germanic tongues, has at all times been governed by what is known as the Germanic accent law, that is by the system of stem accentuation. By this law, except in a few cases, the chief emphasis of the word was thrown on the stem syllable, all others remaining less stressed or entirely unaccented." p.5: "The principle of stem accentuation had been working all through the O.E. period". pp.69-70, sec. 86: "Lastly vowels were shortened for want of stress. Under these are included all those in the second element of compounds and words unaccented in the sentence. O.E. biscopric gave M.E. bishopric, O.E. wisdom was M.E. wisdom."

new_statements.relation_note: Stem accentuation = root/stem-initial main stress, the same placement as the Dresher/Lahiri works, stated as a general Germanic law rather than a ME-specific rule; supplies a traditional-grammar confirmation for the catalog's empty rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: English at all periods, including Middle English, follows the Germanic accent law of stem accentuation: the chief stress falls on the stem syllable and all other syllables are weaker or unstressed (hence the ME levelling of unaccented vowels to e); vowels in the second element of compounds and in sentence-unstressed words were shortened for want of stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as such; second elements of compounds are described only as weakly stressed enough to shorten their vowels (sec. 86).
new_statements.exceptions: 'except in a few cases' (p.3), unspecified; no dedicated accent section, the statement is in the general-features chapter.
